newsitem.title: CHINA: China urges Japan to match island words with deeds.
newsitem.headline: China urges Japan to match island words with deeds.

text.p: Beijing told Tokyo to match words with deeds and stop Japanese rightwingers further inflaming a row over ownership of a group of islands in the East China Sea that claimed its first casualty on Thursday.

The long-running dispute over ownership of the islands, known as the Diaoyus in Chinese and as the Senkakus in Japanese, flared anew when a Hong Kong activist died in the seas near the archipelago while protesting Tokyo's claim.

Japan had said it would curb further action on the islands by nationalist organisations, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing hours after activist David Chan drowned after leaping into the sea from a protest ship.
He said Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda made the promise during a meeting with his Chinese counterpart, Qian Qichen, at the United Nations in New York on Wednesday.
"Foreign Minister Ikeda expressed...(Japan) cannot allow Japanese rightwing groups to take action on the Diaoyu islands issue," Shen said.
"We the Chinese side ask the Japanese side to match its words with deeds," he added.
The dispute flared this month when Japanese rightists moved to buttress Tokyo's claim by repairing a makeshift lighthouse on one of the uninhabited islands.

The row has united nationalist sentiment in China, arch-rival Taiwan and the British colony of Hong Kong, where protests against Japan's control of the potentially resource-rich islands have become common events.

Activist Chan drowned after he leapt into the sea near the islands from the Hong Kong vessel Kien Hwa 2. The chartered vessel had set sail for the islands on Sunday, and had twice entered what Japan considers its territorial waters.
Chan was declared dead when resuscitation efforts by coast guards from a nearby Japanese government ship failed.
On Monday, Japanese patrol ships repulsed a flotilla of activists from rival claimant Taiwan and Hong Kong, which reverts to Beijing rule in mid-1997.

Beijing and Taipei, rivals since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949, agree the Diaoyus have been China's for centuries and dispute Tokyo's claim, which dates to 1895 when Japan defeated imperial China in a war and seized the islands.
Shen said Beijing was looking to Tokyo to cool temperatures over the dispute.
"We hope the Japanese side will take action so that the situation in the area will not continue to deteriorate," he said. He did not give details.
In a related development, China's state-owned China National Offshore Oil Corporation said it welcomed a call from a Japanese company to jointly develop the islands.
"We are, of course, willing to talk with Japan about joint oil exploration in the disputed islands again," a company official said by telephone.
"We raised the suggestion of joint exploration first and held talks with Japan for six years, but the Japan side unilaterally stopped the talks in 1994," he said.
A senior official at Japan's state-run Japan National Oil Corp on Wednesday called for joint exploration, saying cooperation could help ease tensions over the islands.
